subject: Career
title: Eye Contact: The Trust Signal
description: A short lesson to help you apply Eye Contact: The Trust Signal.

hook.text: Too little eye contact signals dishonesty. Too much feels aggressive. The sweet spot is 60-70%.

buildup.text: Research shows moderate eye contact increases perceived trustworthiness and competence.

discovery.text: The trick: look at the interviewer while listening. You can break eye contact while thinking.

twist.text: In video interviews, look at the camera, not the screen. It simulates direct eye contact.

climax.text: Cultural norms vary — in some cultures, direct eye contact with elders is disrespectful.

punchline.text: Eye contact isn't staring. It's connecting.

quiz.question: What percentage of time should you maintain eye contact in interviews?

details.summary: Eye contact activates trust circuits in the brain and signals confidence, engagement, and honesty. In Western interview contexts, maintaining eye contact for sixty to seventy percent of the conversation is perceived as ideal.
details.whyItMatters: Too little eye contact suggests dishonesty or low confidence, while too much feels aggressive. Calibrating eye contact correctly builds rapport and trust throughout the interview.
takeaways: Aim for sixty to seventy percent eye contact during conversation
Look at the triangle between the interviewer's eyes and nose
Break eye contact naturally when thinking to avoid seeming robotic

faq.question: How should eye contact differ in video interviews versus in-person ones?
faq.answer: In video interviews, look at the camera rather than the screen to simulate direct eye contact. This feels unnatural but creates the impression of engagement for the viewer. Periodically glance at the screen to read reactions.

faq.question: What if cultural norms differ on eye contact between interviewer and candidate?
faq.answer: In many East Asian, Middle Eastern, and Indigenous cultures, direct eye contact can signal disrespect. Research the company culture and interviewer background when possible, and generally mirror the level of eye contact the interviewer initiates.
